planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and give seedlings 10–14 days near 50°F once they have several true leaves to encourage earlier, heavier bud set; in zone 9, an August–September sowing for a fall transplant also performs well and often yields the largest buds.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Tavor is a vigorous Israeli-bred F1 hybrid selected for heavy, reliable production of medium, tightly closed green buds on a large, upright, spineless plant, and it is widely favored by growers in hot, dry-summer climates for its strong heat tolerance and steady yield of multiple side buds after the central bud is cut. Like other seed-grown annual types it flowers and produces a usable first-year harvest without needing the extended cold vernalization that older perennial varieties require, though a short cool spell after transplanting still improves bud set and uniformity. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the growing season, and cut buds while still tight and firm, well before the scales begin to loosen and spread.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide

common_name: Colorado Star Artichoke (Cold-Tolerant Purple AAS Winner)

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; Colorado Star sets buds reliably in its first year with only modest cold exposure, making it one of the easier annual artichokes to bring to harvest in a single season without precise vernalization timing.

directions: Start seed indoors and set transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes; Colorado Star is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid bred for reliable first-year flowering across a wide range of climates, including regions with cooler or shorter growing seasons than traditional artichoke territory. Buds are medium-sized with an attractive purple-tinged blush over green, tender at a smaller size than many varieties, and produced in good quantity on a plant more compact than older perennial types, making it a reasonable choice for smaller gardens. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its ease of first-year production from seed. Water regularly and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat, and harvest buds promptly while tightly closed for the best texture and flavor.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide

planting.note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; Opal flowers readily in its first year without a demanding cold-treatment schedule, so a simple cool spell of a couple of weeks after transplanting is generally enough to bring on good bud set.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Opal is an F1 hybrid bred for fast, dependable first-year bud production and stands out for the striking violet-purple color of its rounded, tender buds, which hold their color well even after light cooking. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining strong ornamental appeal with genuine first-year productivity from seed, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for gardeners who want both a harvest and a bold accent plant among vegetables or in a mixed border. Plants are moderately compact for an artichoke and produce a good number of secondary buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest buds while still tightly closed, since the purple color and tender texture are both best before scales begin to loosen.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide
